theory.what: Nagios is an open-source monitoring system that checks hosts and services, sends alerts when problems occur, and provides historical data for analysis. It uses a plugin architecture where each check is a script (Nagios plugin) that returns status codes: OK (0), WARNING (1), CRITICAL (2), UNKNOWN (3). Configuration defines hosts, services (check types), contacts (who gets alerted), time periods (when to check), and escalation rules.
theory.why: Nagios remains widely deployed in enterprise monitoring despite newer alternatives. Its plugin ecosystem (5000+ plugins) can monitor virtually anything. Understanding Nagios is essential for NOC engineers maintaining legacy infrastructure, and the concepts (host checks, service checks, notifications, escalations) apply to all monitoring systems.
theory.how: Nagios Core daemon schedules checks based on check_interval and retry_interval. Passive checks receive results from external systems via NSCA (Nagios Service Check Acceptor). State changes trigger notifications via email, SMS, or custom scripts. Escalation rules ensure the right person is notified at the right time — engineers get alerts first, managers get notified if unacknowledged after N minutes.
theory.when: Nagios is a good choice for: monitoring network devices (ping, interface status, CPU, memory via SNMP), server health (disk, CPU, memory, processes, services), application checks (HTTP response, database connectivity), and environments where the extensive plugin library matches your monitoring needs.
key_concepts: Host and service definitions
Plugin architecture (Nagios Plugins project, 5000+ check scripts)
Active vs passive checks
Notification escalations and contact groups
Flapping detection (state change threshold before alert)
NRPE (Nagios Remote Plugin Executor) for remote checks
Nagios XI (commercial GUI) vs Nagios Core (OSS)
theory.configuration:
define host {
  use        generic-switch
  host_name  Core-SW-01
  address    10.0.0.1
}

define service {
  use                generic-service
  host_name          Core-SW-01
  service_description Uptime
  check_command      check_snmp!-o sysUpTime.0 -w 86400: -c 43200:
  check_interval     5
  retry_interval     1
  notification_interval 60
}
troubleshooting: Alerts not firing: check notification_enabled and notification_options in service/host definitions
False positives: increase retry_interval (check X times before escalation), enable flapping detection
Plugin returns weird output: run the plugin manually from Nagios server command line to verify
NRPE connection refused: check NRPE daemon running on remote host, firewall allowing port 5666
Performance issues with 10000+ checks: use passive checks, distributed monitoring (Nagios satellite servers)
theory.worked_examples: Scenario: Monitoring a network of 100 routers, 200 switches, 50 firewalls. Each device has: ping check (is it alive?), SNMP uptime check (reboot detection), interface status check (all up/down interfaces), CPU and memory utilization (>90% → critical). 350 hosts × 4 services = 1400 checks every 5 minutes = 4.67 checks/second. Nagios handles this fine on a moderate VM (4 vCPU, 8 GB RAM). Escalation setup: Tier 1 NOC gets alerts, if not acknowledged in 15 minutes → Tier 2 senior engineers, if not resolved in 60 minutes → Network Manager. Notification methods: alert pages via email-to-SMS gateway during business hours (timeperiod workhours), PagerDuty integration via custom notification handler for 24/7 critical alerts. PagerDuty handles the call rotation so on-call engineers get phone calls for CRITICAL unacknowledged alerts. Weekly reporting: Nagios provides availability reports — each device's uptime percentage, SLA reporting for management.
theory.summary: Nagios is a foundational monitoring system with concepts (host checks, service checks, notifications, escalations) that apply universally. Master configuration structure, plugin architecture, and NRPE for remote execution. Use passive checks for large-scale monitoring to reduce Nagios server load. Plan notification escalations carefully — alert fatigue is the #1 monitoring failure mode.

theory.what: SNMP traps are unsolicited notifications from network devices to an NMS (Network Management Station). When a significant event occurs (link down, temperature threshold exceeded, authentication failure), the device sends a trap packet to the configured trap receiver (UDP port 162). SNMPv2c traps include a community string and a variable-binding list. SNMPv3 traps add encryption and authentication. Informs (confirmed traps) add reliability with acknowledgment retry.
theory.why: Polling-based monitoring (checking device status every N minutes) has a detection delay equal to the polling interval. A device that goes down 1 second after the last poll won't be detected for 5 minutes (if polling every 5 min). Traps provide immediate notification — sub-second detection of critical events. They also reduce polling load: a device with 50 monitored interfaces can send a trap for 'interface down' instead of being polled for 50 interface statuses.
theory.how: Devices send traps to the NMS trap receiver at UDP 162. The NMS must listen on port 162. Common trap types: linkUp/linkDown (interface status change), coldStart/warmStart (device reboot), authenticationFailure (failed SNMP access), and enterprise-specific traps (vendor-defined events like BGP neighbor down on Cisco). The NMS correlates traps with device state: a linkDown trap updates the device's interface status to 'down' in the monitoring database.
theory.when: SNMP traps are essential for real-time network monitoring: interface state changes, device reboots, environmental alerts (temperature, fan failure), security events (invalid login attempts), and BGP/OSPF neighbor state changes. Most NMS platforms (Nagios, Zabbix, SolarWinds, PRTG) include trap receivers.
key_concepts: Trap vs Inform: traps are unacknowledged (UDP, fire-and-forget), informs are acknowledged (TCP-like retry)
SNMPv2c traps: community string for authentication (plaintext, not secure)
SNMPv3 traps: authNoPriv, authPriv (with encryption)
Enterprise-specific traps: unique OIDs defined by vendors (Cisco, Juniper)
Trap receiver configuration on NMS: listen on UDP 162
Trap severity mapping: linkDown = critical, authenticationFailure = warning, coldStart = critical
theory.configuration:
# Device configuration
snmp-server host 10.0.0.100 version 2c NETOPS
snmp-server enable traps snmp linkdown linkup
snmp-server enable traps ospf state-change
snmp-server enable traps bgp
snmp-server enable traps config
!
# NMS (snmptrapd.conf)
authCommunity NETOPS
format theEvent $A $a $N $n $w $W $c $C $F $T
troubleshooting: No traps received: verify UDP 162 reachable from device to NMS, check snmp-server enable traps for the specific trap type
Traps received but not processed: verify trap receiver is running on port 162, check for port conflicts (multiple NMS instances)
Too many traps (trap storm): configure trap rate-limiting on devices (snmp-server trap-timeout 30)
SNMPv3 authentication failure: verify user credentials and authentication protocol (MD5/SHA) match on both sides
Trap OID not recognized: update MIB files on NMS (download vendor MIBs for enterprise-specific traps)
theory.worked_examples: Scenario: NOC monitoring 500 network devices. Monitoring platform receives 5,000+ traps/hour. A core switch port goes down: 1) Device sends linkDown trap to NMS (UDP 162) within 50ms of detecting the failure, 2) NMS trap receiver processes: correlates with device inventory, interface name (Gig0/1), connected device info (from LLDP topology), 3) Updates the device's interface status to 'down' in the monitoring database, 4) Triggers alerting: if this is the only uplink to a critical server, NMS sends PagerDuty notification immediately. Without traps: next poll cycle (5 min later) shows interface down. Trap-based detection: 50ms vs 5 minutes = 99.98% faster detection. Trap storm scenario: a power outage causes 50 switches to reboot simultaneously — 50 coldStart traps arrive in under a second. Trap receiver rate-limits processing: queues traps, deduplicates by device, creates a single incident for '50 devices rebooted' vs 50 individual alerts.
theory.summary: SNMP traps provide immediate event notification for critical network events. Configure devices to send traps for link state changes, device reboots, and protocol events. Use snmptrapd or integrate with your NMS platform's trap receiver. Plan for trap storms (power events, widespread failures) with rate limiting and deduplication. Prefer SNMPv3 with authPriv for security.

theory.what: Automated configuration backup collects device running/startup configurations on a schedule (typically daily) and stores them in version control (Git). Tools: Oxidized (Ruby-based, powerful filtering and hooks), RANCID (original tool, Perl-based, supports extensive device types), and custom scripts using Ansible/Netmiko. Backups are automatically committed to Git, providing a full history of every configuration change.
theory.why: Manual config backups are forgotten, inconsistent, and don't provide change history. Automated backups are essential for: disaster recovery (restore a device from its last known-good config), change audit (who changed what and when), compliance (PCI DSS requires 12-month config history), and troubleshooting (compare config before/after an incident).
theory.how: Oxidized connects to devices via SSH/Telnet and runs 'show running-config' (or vendor-equivalent). It parses the output, filters sensitive data (passwords can be removed), and writes to a Git repository. Web interface (Oxidized-Web) provides diff views between versions. Hooks can trigger notifications on config changes (Slack, email). RANCID uses expect scripts to login and collect configs from devices of different vendors.
theory.when: Automated config backup is mandatory for any production network with more than 5 devices. Implement during initial deployment, not as an afterthought. Essential for: change management (see exactly what changed), disaster recovery (restore from backup), security audit (monitor for unauthorized changes), and compliance (SOC 2, PCI DSS, HIPAA all require config change tracking).
key_concepts: Git-based version control for full change history
Oxidized: modern, Ruby-based with web interface support
RANCID: legacy but extensive device-type support
Schedule frequency (typically daily, some critical devices every hour)
Sensitive data filtering (remove passwords from stored configs)
Hooks for Slack/email notifications on config changes
Diff view between consecutive versions
theory.configuration:
# Oxidized config
username: netops
password: <encrypted>
model: ios
interval: 86400
use_svn: false
output:
  file:
    directory: /var/lib/oxidized/configs
hooks:
  slack_diff:
    type: slackdiff
    auth_token: xoxb-xxx
    channel: '#network-changes'
    diff: true
troubleshooting: Backup failure for specific device: check SSH access, verify credentials, test with 'oxidized <device-ip>' manually
Git repository too large: use shallow clone, compress old history with git gc
Password visible in Git: enable remove_secret filter in Oxidized config, scrub existing Git history with git filter-branch
Timeouts on slow devices: increase timeout in Oxidized config, disable DNS resolution with 'input: ssh: dns: false'
Backup shows no change when change exists: verify the device's running-config actually persists — some changes don't take effect until 'copy running-config startup-config'
theory.worked_examples: Scenario: 200-device network with daily Oxidized backups to Git. Monday at 10:15 AM: a core router experiences BGP peering failures. NOC checks Oxidized Git log: 'router-core-01 running Sun 22:00 — commit 9942f5, Mon 08:15 — commit a1b2c3'. A diff shows: the Monday commit has 'no router bgp 65000' added — someone removed the BGP configuration! Git blame shows the commit author was the junior engineer who had SSH access. The engineer's change ticket referenced 'cleaning up old config'. Investigation: they accidentally removed BGP while cleaning up OSPF test configs. Recovery: git revert a1b2c3 and re-deploy the config via Oxidized (hook runs Ansible to push config back). Service restored in 8 minutes vs hours without config backup. Oxidized also captured that the junior engineer made 3 other config changes that morning — all reviewed and one additional problem found (removed ACL entry).
theory.summary: Automated config backup is the most impactful monitoring investment for any network. Use Oxidized or RANCID with Git backend for full version history of all device configurations. Filter sensitive data, use hooks for real-time change notifications, and integrate with ticketing to correlate config changes with incidents. Practice restore procedures from backup regularly.

theory.what: Capacity forecasting predicts future network resource needs based on historical utilization trends. It uses time-series analysis of metrics like bandwidth utilization, CPU, memory, disk, port count, and power consumption. Methods range from simple linear regression (assuming current growth continues) to Holt-Winters exponential smoothing (accounts for seasonality — daily/weekly/monthly patterns) and ARIMA (AutoRegressive Integrated Moving Average) for complex patterns.
theory.why: Capacity exhaustion causes outages: a WAN link at 95% utilization will experience packet loss during traffic bursts, a switch at 90% CPU will drop routing updates. Reactive capacity management (upgrade when it breaks) causes incidents. Proactive forecasting gives 3-6 month lead time to budget, procure, and install capacity upgrades before the resource is exhausted.
theory.how: Collect historical utilization data (min, max, average for each metric) from monitoring systems (SNMP, NetFlow, telemetry). Plot the data, identify trends (linear, exponential, or seasonal). Apply the appropriate forecasting model: linear regression for steady growth, Holt-Winters for seasonal traffic (e.g., month-end spikes for retail). Calculate exhaustion date: when does the trend line intersect the capacity limit (e.g., 80% utilization threshold).
theory.when: Capacity forecasting is essential for: WAN links (bandwidth growth, 6-month forecast), data center power and cooling (server refresh cycles), internet bandwidth (10-30% annual growth is typical), switch port utilization (adding new IDFs), and MPLS VPN circuit growth. Do quarterly reviews for critical infrastructure.
key_concepts: Utilization thresholds: 80% normal max, 100% max = packet loss
Linear vs exponential vs seasonal trends
Holt-Winters exponential smoothing for seasonal data
Confidence intervals (predictions have error bands)
Data collection frequency (5-minute averages vs daily max)
Capacity lead time (procurement + installation + testing)
troubleshooting: Trend line doesn't fit data: check for outliers (migration events, new site openings) that skew growth
Predictions too high/low: extend data window to 12+ months, validate against actuals monthly
Seasonal patterns missed: use weekly data not daily for short-term trends, monthly for long-term
Capacity already saturated: emergency expedite (overnight shipping for optics, 24-hour turn up), prioritize over standard forecast
theory.worked_examples: Scenario: WAN link from HQ to colo runs at 60% average, 85% peak. Monthly data over 12 months shows traffic growing linearly at ~3% per month (36% annual growth). Simple forecast: 60% + 3% × months → 7 months to reach 80% (recommended upgrade trigger), 13 months to reach 100% (exhaustion). Lead time for circuit upgrade (ISP provisioning): 45-60 days. Decision: order circuit upgrade in month 5 (2 months before 80% threshold) from 1 Gbps to 10 Gbps. Actual result: at month 7, utilization metric shows 82% peak — right on forecast. Upgrade installed at month 8, peak utilization drops to 8.2% on 10 Gbps link. Refinement: Holt-Winters model showed 5% monthly growth during business hours but 1% overnight. Using business-hours-only data (which drives the upgrade decision), the forecast was more accurate. Segregating by traffic type: voice traffic flat (stable), data traffic growing 5%/month (SaaS application adoption), backup traffic growing 8%/month (more servers backing up to cloud). Result: data and backup traffic growth is the driver — consider on-prem backup caching (reduces WAN backup traffic by 70%) to extend circuit life by 18 months.
theory.summary: Capacity forecasting prevents outages by predicting resource exhaustion before it happens. Collect 12+ months of utilization data, apply appropriate models (linear for steady growth, Holt-Winters for seasonal patterns), and plan upgrades with procurement lead time included. Review forecasts quarterly and validate predictions against actuals monthly. Always consider traffic-shaping or optimization before pure capacity upgrades.

theory.what: NOC runbooks are step-by-step documented procedures for handling common network incidents and operational tasks. They include: symptoms (what alert triggered this), severity classification (P1-P4), initial diagnosis steps, troubleshooting decision trees (if symptom A → test B → if B fails → do C), resolution procedures, escalation criteria and contacts, post-resolution verification steps, and incident tracking requirements.
theory.why: Without runbooks, incident response quality varies by engineer experience — a junior engineer may take 2 hours to solve what a senior could fix in 10 minutes. Runbooks standardize response: every engineer follows the same proven procedure, reducing MTTR by 50-70% for documented incidents. They also enable shift handoffs (team A can follow runbook without waking up team B) and serve as training material for new NOC hires.
theory.how: Runbooks are typically maintained in a wiki (Confluence, Notion, Git repository with Markdown). Each incident type has its own runbook. Decision trees use if/then/else logic visible in the flow. Common runbook sections: Alert Description, Severity, Devices Affected, Initial Checks, Troubleshooting Flow (decision tree), Resolution Steps, Escalation Path, Post-Resolution Checks. Best-practice runbooks are tested and validated — if a runbook step doesn't work, an incident ticket creates a runbook fix.
theory.when: Runbooks should exist for: all P1/P2 alert types (link down, BGP down, high CPU, high latency), recurring incidents (the ones that generate most tickets), on-call procedures (how to acknowledge, update, hand off), maintenance procedures (how to add VLAN, update firmware), and disaster recovery procedures (full site failover). Every new incident type should produce a runbook within 2 weeks.
key_concepts: Decision trees for symptom-to-resolution mapping
Severity classification: P1 (critical, <4 hrs), P2 (high, <8 hrs), P3 (medium, <24 hrs), P4 (low, <72 hrs)
Escalation criteria and contacts with SLA timers
Runbook version control (Git-based, reviewed quarterly)
Automation hooks (runbooks that trigger Ansible scripts)
Post-incident runbook updates (lessons learned → runbook improvement)
theory.configuration:
# Example runbook structure
## BGP Peering Down
Severity: P1 | MTTR Target: <30 min

### Symptoms
- PagerDuty alert: 'BGP session down'
- Customer reports routing issues to remote site

### Initial Checks
1. Check show ip bgp summary on both routers
2. Verify local interface is up/up (show interface)
3. Ping the neighbor IP

### Decision Tree
▶ Neighbor reachable?
  YES → Check BGP config mismatch (ASN, hold timer)
  NO → Check L1 (fiber, optics, cross-connect)

### Resolution
1. If config mismatch: correct BGP parameters
2. If fiber issue: engage transport provider, reroute

### Escalation
PagerDuty auto-escalates to senior engineer after 15 min
troubleshooting: Runbook steps don't work as documented: flag for review, create fix PR, no-runbook-knowledge/incident-treatment
Engineers not following runbook: make them the default (pager notification includes runbook URL), audit incident tickets for runbook adherence
Runbooks out of date: schedule quarterly review cycle, use incident post-mortems as update triggers
Too many runbooks to maintain: prioritize by incident frequency × severity, P1/P2 incidents must have runbooks
theory.worked_examples: Scenario: P1 alert — 'Core Router Interface Down'. Runbook steps: 1) Verify which interface (show interface Gig0/0), 2) Check interface status (is it up/down, admin down, err-disabled?), 3) If up/down → check CRC errors (high CRC = bad optics/ fiber), 4) If CRC > 10/sec → replace SFP from hot-spare (resolved in 8 min), 5) If no CRC errors → check remote end interface status (is fiber cut?), 6) If remote end also down → open transport provider ticket, 7) Route traffic manually: change OSPF cost on remaining uplink to direct traffic through backup path. Following the runbook: junior engineer (2 weeks on the job) resolves the incident in 12 minutes (SFP replacement). Without runbook: would have escalated immediately to senior (who's on another call) — MTTR would have been 35+ minutes. Post-incident: runbook updated with SFP part number and hot-spare location (cabinet 3, shelf B).
theory.summary: NOC runbooks are essential for consistent, rapid incident response. Document every recurring incident type with decision trees, escalation criteria, and resolution steps. Keep runbooks in version control and review quarterly. Every new incident generates or updates a runbook. Measure runbook adherence and MTTR improvement to demonstrate value.

theory.what: Event correlation is the process of relating individual alerts and events to identify root cause and reduce noise. A single fiber cut may generate 10,000 events (router interfaces down, BGP sessions down, application errors, monitoring polls timing out). Correlation groups these as one incident: 'Site A fiber cut affecting 200 services.' Methods include: temporal (events within N minutes), topological (events on same device or connected devices), rule-based (if event A + event B → new event C), and AI/ML (pattern recognition from historical data).
theory.why: Without correlation, NOC engineers drown in alert noise. Statistics: a single network failure can generate 1000+ alerts. Engineers develop alert fatigue, ignoring critical alerts among the noise. Correlation reduces 1000 alerts to 1 root cause incident, enabling fast, focused response. Correlation also identifies secondary issues (a firewall failover triggered by the primary failure).
theory.how: Monitoring platforms (Nagios, Zabbix, Splunk, ServiceNow ITOM) implement correlation engines. Temporal correlation: events within 5-minute sliding window with matching device/group are grouped. Topological correlation: events from devices sharing a parent (same switch, same circuit, same site) are grouped. Rule-based correlation: 'If Router-A interface down AND Router-B interface down AND both connect to same circuit → root cause is circuit failure' (suppress all other Router-A/B events).
theory.when: Event correlation is essential for any NOC processing 10,000+ events/day. It's critical during major incidents (correlate thousands of events into one incident timeline) and for recurring partial failures (correlate 50 'interface flapping' events into one 'bad SFP in Distribution-3' incident).
key_concepts: Temporal correlation (time-window based grouping)
Topological correlation (device hierarchy based grouping)
Rule-based correlation (if-then deduction)
Compression (repeated same event → single incident with count)
Suppression (suppress child events when parent event detected)
Deduplication (same event from same source within N minutes = one alert)
Root cause analysis (RCA) through correlation
troubleshooting: False correlation grouping two unrelated incidents: adjust time window narrower, add more specific topological constraints
Missing correlation (events not grouped): widen time window, add correlation rules for known event patterns
Correlation rules too complex: start with simple temporal + topological, add rule-based gradually
Performance issues with 100K+ events: pre-filter noise events before correlation engine, use streaming correlation
theory.worked_examples: Scenario: Fiber cut between HQ and Data Center at 2 PM. Events received by NMS in a 30-second window: 1) Link-down trap from Router-HQ Gig0/1 (connected to DC), 2) BGP session down alert (neighbor 10.0.0.2), 3) Link-down trap from Router-DC Gig0/0 (connected to HQ), 4) OSPF adjacency change (neighbor 10.0.0.2 down), 5) 150 SNMP polling timeouts for DC devices, 6) 200 application health check failures. Correlation engine: Topological rule detects Router-HQ Gig0/1 and Router-DC Gig0/0 are connected to circuit 'HQ-DC-Fiber-001'. Temporal: all events within 30s window. Rule-based: 'IF linkDown on both ends of circuit X AND BGP session over X down THEN root cause = circuit X failure'. Output: one incident 'Circuit HQ-DC-Fiber-001 down — 355 correlated events suppressed'. NOC sees 1 alert, not 355. Secondary correlation: automatic reroute detected (traffic now via backup path with increased latency) — creates P2 incident 'WAN Latency Increased' linked to the P1 circuit failure. Without correlation: NOC would be flooded with 355 alerts, delaying actual root cause identification by 5-10 minutes.
theory.summary: Event correlation is the key to NOC sanity at scale. Start with temporal and topological correlation (easy to implement, big impact), then add rule-based for complex scenarios. Target: 90%+ alert reduction during major incidents. Monitor correlation accuracy (false correlations) and refine rules quarterly. Good correlation means the NOC can focus on fixing problems, not filtering noise.

theory.what: Network weather maps provide real-time visualization of network utilization overlaid on a topology map. Links are color-coded by utilization (green < 25%, yellow < 50%, orange < 75%, red < 90%, black = critical). Tools like PRTG, SolarWinds, LibreNMS, and Cacti produce weather maps. The map shows the physical or logical topology with live utilization data updated every 1-5 minutes.
theory.why: Raw utilization numbers in tables are hard to process quickly. A weather map gives instant visual status: a NOC engineer can glance at the map and immediately see the congested link (red) between HQ and DC. Weather maps reduce time-to-awareness from seconds (reading tables) to milliseconds (seeing color), enabling faster response to developing congestion.
theory.how: Weather maps collect SNMP interface statistics (ifInOctets, ifOutOctets) every polling interval (usually 5 minutes). They calculate utilization as a percentage of interface bandwidth and color-code the link. Maps are typically laid out geographically (site map with real floor plan) or logically (network topology diagram). Bandwidth calculations use the formula: bits_per_second = (delta_counter × 8) / delta_time.
theory.when: Weather maps are valuable for: NOC wall displays (big-screen visualization showing network health-at-a-glance), capacity planning (visually identifying hot spots), shift handoffs (quick status overview with charts), and executive reports (simple, visual network health indicators).
key_concepts: Utilization-based color coding (green → yellow → orange → red → black)
Topology overlay (physical or logical layout)
Real-time data collection via SNMP (ifInOctets/ifOutOctets)
Capacity vs utilization (bandwidth x percent used)
Historical playback (replay the map for any point in time)
NOC wall dashboard (large screen, cycling through maps)

Too many maps to maintain: prioritize by criticality (core network > distribution > access)
theory.worked_examples: Scenario: NOC wall display showing 6 weather maps cycling every 30 seconds: WAN connectivity (8 sites), Campus core (3 distribution blocks), Data Center fabric (leaf-spine topology), Internet edge (2 ISPs, 4 BGP peers), Customer connections (MPLS VRF mappings), Power/cooling (PDU temperature overlay). During a busy period, the Duty Manager sees the WAN map showing a link turning orange (65% utilization) between HQ and DC — climbing to red (85%) over 10 minutes. Without weather map: this slow congestion would only be noticed when a user complains (30+ min delay). With weather map: engineer sees the trend, investigates, finds a backup job running that should be scheduled for off-peak — the backup is paused, utilization returns to 25%. The weather map visualization was key to the 10-minute detection vs 30+ minute user-driven detection.
theory.summary: Weather maps provide instant visual network health status for NOC environments. Use SNMP-based polling for utilization data, color-code links by utilization percentage, and display on NOC wall displays. Focus weather map design on the most critical network paths rather than trying to map every link. Supplement with historical playback for trend analysis.

theory.what: On-call management structures 24/7 incident response with rotating schedules, escalation policies, and response SLAs. PagerDuty, OpsGenie, and xMatters are the primary platforms. Schedules define primary and secondary coverage (typically 1-2 week rotations). Escalation policies define who gets notified when and how (push notification → phone call → manager escalation). Response SLAs: P1 <15 min acknowledge, <1 hour engineer on it; P2 <30 min acknowledge.
theory.why: Networks run 24/7. Without structured on-call, every engineer is effectively always on-call (burnout), response times are unpredictable, and incidents fall through cracks (no one knows who's responsible at 3 AM). Structured on-call ensures: clear ownership (the primary knows it's their week), defined response times (SLA targets), fair rotation (workload distributed equitably), and escalation paths (auto-escalate if primary doesn't respond).
theory.how: PagerDuty rotation: schedule defines weekly rotation (primary, secondary). When an alert fires, it pages the primary via push notification. If no acknowledgement in 10 minutes, escalates to secondary. If still no response after 10 more minutes, calls the primary (phone call with automated voice). If unacknowledged after 30 minutes, escalates to on-call manager. Overrides handle PTO (substitute engineer assigned for specific days).
theory.when: On-call management is essential for any NOC or IT team supporting production infrastructure 24/7. Implement for: network operations (link down at 3 AM), system administration (server failure on weekend), database administration (replication lag at midnight), and DevOps (production incident at any hour).
key_concepts: Rotation schedules (weekly, 2-week, or daily)
Primary and secondary/backup roles
Escalation policies with timed steps
Acknowledgement and response SLAs
Overrides for PTO and schedule swaps
Follow-the-sun (US → EMEA → APAC handoffs)
On-call fatigue management (rotation size, compensation)
theory.configuration:
# PagerDuty config (conceptual)
schedule:

  start_time: 2024-01-01T09:00:00Z

troubleshooting: Engineers not responding on-call: review escalation compliance, address with team, check PagerDuty mobile app configuration

theory.worked_examples: Scenario: 8-person network team, weekly on-call rotation. Each engineer is primary one week every 8 weeks (reasonable load). PagerDuty configured: P1 (critical) → push notification → 10 min → call primary → 15 min → escalate to secondary → 10 min → call manager. Average weekly on-call: 5-10 alerts (P1-P3), 1-2 mid-night P1s. Monday morning: primary engineer wakes up to 3 P1 pages from weekend — a fiber cut Friday night was resolved, but two secondary alerts were duplicate noise. Post-mortem identifies that the fiber cut triggered both the circuit alert AND a BGP session alert for the same root cause. Correlation rule added: suppress BGP alerts when corresponding circuit alert fires. Alert volume drops from 8/week to 6/week. After implementing better correlation, P1 alerts drop to 3-4/week. On-call quality of life improves significantly — engineers can sleep through most nights. Team satisfaction score increases from 3.2 to 4.1/5.
theory.summary: Structured on-call management prevents burnout and ensures reliable incident response. Use PagerDuty or similar with clear rotation schedules, multi-level escalations, and response SLAs. Audit alert noise regularly — every non-actionable alert degrades on-call quality. Maintain minimum rotation sizes (8+ for reasonable workload) and provide fair compensation for on-call duty.

theory.what: Maintenance windows are scheduled periods during which planned changes can be made to network infrastructure with minimal business impact. They specify: start/end time (typically off-peak — 2 AM Sunday), scope (which devices/services are affected), expected impact (brief connectivity loss, no traffic loss), rollback plan (how to revert within the window), and approval chain (who authorized the change). Change management systems (ServiceNow, Jira) track maintenance windows.
theory.why: Without maintenance windows, urgent changes happen during business hours causing user impact. Scheduled windows enable: predictable impact (users know Sunday 2-4 AM means possible brief outages), thorough planning (pre-change testing, rollback procedures, impact analysis), approval workflow (prevent unauthorized changes), and freeze periods during peak business times (holiday shopping, quarter-end close).
theory.how: Change management workflow: RFC (Request for Change) created with scope, risk assessment, implementation plan, rollback plan. Change advisory board (CAB) meeting reviews RFCs (typically weekly). Approved changes are scheduled in a maintenance window. Prior to the window: engineer sends reminder to stakeholders (24h before), pre-change checks are verified (backup config, verify rollback steps). During the window: engineer implements change, verifies operation, validates with monitoring. Post-window: send completion notification, update documentation.
theory.when: Maintenance windows are required for: firmware upgrades (IOS upgrade requires reboot), hardware replacement (line card, SFP, PSU), routing protocol changes (BGP policy, OSPF metrics), network segmentation changes (new VLAN across multiple switches), and any change affecting production traffic. Emergency changes (security patches, outage fix) can bypass normal window with expedited approval.
key_concepts: RFC (Request for Change) with scope, plan, rollback
CAB (Change Advisory Board) for approval
Risk assessment (low/medium/high — affects window approval)
Freeze periods (no changes during critical business times)
Rollback plan (must be tested before window)
Post-change verification (monitoring, testing, user validation)
Change communication (24h notice, completion notification)
theory.configuration:
# ServiceNow Change Request form (conceptual)
Short Description: "IOS Upgrade — Core-SW-01, Core-SW-02"
Risk Level: Medium
Planned Start: 2024-01-15 02:00 UTC
Planned End: 2024-01-15 04:00 UTC
Scope: Core switches in DC1
Implementation Plan: 
  1. Backup running-config
  2. Copy IOS image to flash
  3. Reload Core-SW-01 (30min)
  4. Verify OSPF adjacency with Core-SW-02
  5. Repeat for Core-SW-02
Rollback Plan: boot system flash:old-ios.bin; reload
CAB Approval: Pending
troubleshooting: Change takes longer than window: implement rollback plan if exceeding 80% of window time, schedule remaining work next window
Change fails: execute rollback plan immediately (within window), don't deviate from tested rollback
Change noticed by users: verify communication list was correct, add missing stakeholders to future notifications
Emergency change needed outside window: expedited CAB approval via email, document with post-change review
Frequent changes to same device: aggregate into single larger window rather than weekly small changes
theory.worked_examples: Scenario: Firmware upgrade of 4 core switches from IOS 15.2 to 17.3 (security patches). Planned window: Saturday 2-6 AM (4 hours). Pre-change: 1) RFC approved at weekly CAB meeting, 2) 48-hour reminder sent to all stakeholders (IT, facilities, building management), 3) Backups of all 4 switches taken and verified, 4) New IOS image copied to all switches and verified (show file), 5) Console access tested (out-of-band), 6) Rollback plan confirmed (old IOS still on flash). During window: 1) Core-SW-01 reloaded — OSFP adjacency lost for 45 seconds (expected), 2) Core-SW-01 comes back with new IOS — OSPF adjacency re-established within 15 seconds (verify with show ip ospf neighbor), 3) Verify VLANs, STP, HSRP — all normal, 4) Continue with remaining 3 switches sequentially, 5) Complete at 3:45 AM (15 min early). Post-change: verify all interfaces up, all BGP peers established, all HSRP groups active. Send completion notice. Observed: one switch had an interface that didn't come up (no light) — SFP reseated, came up. This was in the rollback plan as 'Interface not up: reseat SFP' — completed within 2 minutes, no window extension needed.
theory.summary: Maintenance windows provide structure for safe network changes. Every change needs: clear scope, tested implementation plan, verified rollback plan, stakeholder communication, and CAB approval. Respect window boundaries — roll back if exceeding 80% of window. Document all changes and post-change results. Implement freeze periods during critical business times. Emergency changes exist for urgent needs but require expedited approval.

theory.what: Vendor/ISP management covers the processes and documentation for managing relationships with service providers and equipment vendors. It includes: circuit inventory (circuit IDs, carriers, bandwidth, demarcation points, SLA parameters), escalation contacts (NOC-to-NOC, account managers, engineering contacts), maintenance contracts (hardware support, software subscriptions, renewal dates), and SLA tracking (availability guarantees, credits for violations).
theory.why: When a WAN circuit fails, the difference between a 20-minute fix and a 4-hour fix is often knowing who to call and what information to provide. Vendor management ensures every circuit has: carrier name, circuit ID, contact number, and SLA response time — documented and accessible. Without this, engineers waste time finding the right contact while the circuit is down.
theory.how: A vendor management database (VMDb) tracks: circuit ID (carrier's unique identifier), carrier NOC phone/email, SLA response time (4 hours for critical, 8 hours for standard), account manager contact, contract renewal date (avoid auto-renewal surprises), service location (building, floor, room, rack), demarcation point (where carrier responsibility ends). SLA credits: carriers credit 1-10% of monthly fee for SLA violations (track in a spreadsheet and claim quarterly).
theory.when: Vendor management is essential for: any organization with 5+ ISP/MPLS circuits, when managing multiple carriers and technologies (MPLS, DIA, LTE backup, SD-WAN), when contracts are being negotiated (competitive bidding, renewal negotiation), and when auditing SLAs (ensuring carriers meet commitments).
key_concepts: Circuit inventory database (carrier, circuit ID, bandwidth, location, SLA)
Escalation contacts with tiers (T1 NOC → T2 engineer → account manager)
SLA monitoring and credit claiming
Contract lifecycle management (renewal dates, termination notice periods)
Demarcation point and responsibility boundaries
Competitive bidding (RFP process for carrier selection)

theory.worked_examples: Scenario: Company has 15 circuits from 5 carriers — MPLS, DIA, and LTE backup at 8 sites. A critical MPLS circuit at the primary data center goes down at 10 PM. With good vendor management: NOC engineer looks up the circuit in inventory — finds circuit ID 'MPLS-CORP-001', AT&T carrier NOC 1-800-555-0100, escalation path (T1 → T2 within 30 min), and SLA (4-hour response, 99.99% availability). Engineer calls AT&T with circuit ID ready → AT&T dispatches field tech to the correct demarc location (Rack C, Panel 2, Port 1 at 100 Data Center Drive) — correct site, correct room. Circuit restored in 2.5 hours. Post-incident: SLA credit claimed — $500 for 2.5 hours > 4-hour SLA violation (99.99% = 52 minutes/month allowed downtime, and this was 2.5 hours). Without vendor management: engineer would spend 30+ minutes finding the circuit info, possibly calling the wrong carrier or wrong NOC number. MTTR increases from 2.5 to 3+ hours.
theory.summary: Vendor/ISP management is critical for efficient incident response with carrier circuits. Maintain a comprehensive circuit inventory database with circuit IDs, NOC contacts, SLA parameters, and contract renewal dates. Proactively monitor SLA compliance and claim credits for violations. Standardize on fewer carriers where possible for simpler management at scale.

theory.what: Network Disaster Recovery (DR) plans ensure network services can be restored after a major failure — natural disaster (fire, flood, earthquake), facility loss (power outage, HVAC failure), or cyber attack (ransomware, DDoS). Key metrics: RTO (Recovery Time Objective — how fast to restore, target 4 hours), RPO (Recovery Point Objective — how much data loss acceptable, target 15 minutes). DR includes: DR site (secondary data center or colocation), failover procedures (DNS, BGP, Anycast), backup connectivity (secondary ISP, LTE failover), and documented recovery steps.
theory.why: Without a DR plan, a single facility loss can take down the entire network for days. 40% of businesses that experience a major IT failure without a DR plan never recover. The plan must be tested — untested DR plans fail 70% of the time during actual disasters (the plan has gaps, outdated contacts, wrong steps).
theory.how: DR tiers: Active-Active (both sites live, instant failover), Active-Passive (DR site on standby, failover in minutes/hours), Cold (DR site requires equipment installation, failover in days). DNS failover: low TTL (60-300s) on public DNS records, health-check-based failover. BGP failover: advertise same IP prefix from both sites with AS path prepending to prefer primary. Backup connectivity: LTE/5G failover at each site (automatic VPN tunnel activation when primary circuit fails).
theory.when: DR planning is essential for: any Tier 3+ data center (regulated industry, financial services), single-site operations (no DR = business-ending risk), and organizations with regulatory recovery requirements (PCI DSS requires tested DR annually, HIPAA requires contingency plan).
key_concepts: RTO (Recovery Time Objective) and RPO (Recovery Point Objective)
Active-Active vs Active-Passive vs Cold DR tiers
DNS failover with health checks and low TTL
BGP anycast for IP-level failover
Backup connectivity (LTE, satellite, secondary ISP)
DR testing types: walkthrough, tabletop, simulated, full failover
Runbook for DR (step-by-step failover and recovery)
theory.configuration:
# BGP DR failover configuration (primary site)
route-map SET-AS-PATH permit 10
 set as-path prepend 65000 65000 65000
!
router bgp 65000
 network 203.0.113.0 mask 255.255.255.0
 neighbor 10.0.0.1 route-map SET-AS-PATH out
# DR site advertises same prefix without prepend (shorter path)
troubleshooting: Failover to DR site doesn't work: test with actual circuit disconnect, not simulation — DR drills must include real traffic cutover
DNS failover too slow: lower TTL to 60 seconds 24 hours before expected failover, use health-check with 10-second intervals
DR site capacity insufficient: test with actual production load, not just device availability
DR plan out of date: schedule full DR test annually, partial tests quarterly
Team doesn't know DR steps: run tabletop exercises (walk through the runbook as a team, identify gaps)
theory.worked_examples: Scenario: Financial services company with production data center in New Jersey, DR site in Dallas. Annual DR test: 1) Pre-test preparation: TTL lowered on all public DNS records to 60 seconds (24 hours before test). 2) Backup connectivity verified: LTE failover at both sites tested. 3) Saturday 10 AM: simulate NJ DC failure — push button to stop BGP advertisements from NJ. 4) DNS health checks detect NJ failure (3 consecutive failures, 10-second interval = 30 seconds). 5) Route 53 fails over all production DNS records to Dallas IPs. 6) DR site BGP advertisement takes over — traffic arrives at Dallas. 7) Applications checked: all critical apps (trading, database, web) operational within 90 seconds via Dallas. 8) Post-test review: 2 out of 15 internal apps had DNS resolution issues (used A records with 24-hour TTL instead of Route 53 alias records) — fixed. Full failover in 90 seconds vs RTO target of 4 hours. Annual DR test identified 3 issues in 2024 (DNS TTL for internal apps, stale DR config on 2 switches, missing LTE SIM cards at one site) that were fixed before a real disaster.
theory.summary: Network DR is the insurance policy against catastrophic failure. Define RTO/RPO targets, implement Active-Active or Active-Passive architecture, and test the plan regularly. Annual full failover tests are essential — an untested DR plan is not a DR plan. Include DNS, BGP, application, and staff procedural testing in DR exercises. Document everything in a DR runbook (step-by-step, tested in the last drill).

theory.what: Network inventory management tracks all physical and logical network assets: devices (routers, switches, firewalls, load balancers), serial numbers, locations (building, floor, rack, U position), software versions, warranty/contract status, EOL/EOS dates, interface connections (cable management), and spares inventory. Tools: NetBox (open-source) or DCIM solutions (ServiceNow, Device42, Sunbird DCIM).
theory.why: Can't manage what you don't know. Inventory management answers: 'How many 10 Gbps SFP+ optics do we have in stock?' (procurement), 'Which switches have software version 15.2 and need security patching?' (compliance), 'Is this switch under warranty?' (repair cost), and 'Where is the spare for the core switch?' (disaster recovery). Without inventory, each question requires hours of investigation.
theory.how: NetBox models: Sites → Racks → Devices → Modules → Interfaces → Cables → Power Outlets → Circuits. Each device entry includes: manufacturer, model, serial number, asset tag, rack position (U number, front/back), software version, status (active, planned, decommissioning), and custom fields (contract number, warranty expiration). Discovery tools (Oxidized, LibreNMS, SNMP scans) can auto-populate parts of the inventory.
theory.when: Inventory management is essential for: organizations with 50+ network devices (hard to track manually), compliance requirements (PCI DSS, SOC 2 require asset inventory), lifecycle management (tracking EOL/EOS dates for refresh planning), and any organization that needs to know 'what devices do we have and where are they?'.
key_concepts: Asset lifecycle: procurement → deployment → operation → decommission
Rack elevation (U position, front/rear of rack)
Cable management (patch panel port → switch port mapping)
EOL/EOS tracking (vendor End-of-Life/End-of-Support dates)
Spares inventory (hot spares, cold spares, on-vendor-repair)
Contract/warranty tracking (support levels, renewal dates)
Auto-discovery vs manual entry (auto-discovery from SNMP, manual for physical details)

troubleshooting: Inventory out of date: schedule quarterly audits — physically verify devices match inventory records
Duplicates from auto-discovery: configure device identification rules (hostname pattern, sysName OID match), merge duplicates
Missing serial numbers: most devices expose serial via SNMP (entPhysicalSerialNum), auto-discover and populate
Cable management complexity: use structured cable naming (Site-Floor-Panel-Port), color-code cable labels
Spares not found when needed: track spares as inventory items with location, not just as 'in the closet'
theory.worked_examples: Scenario: 500 devices across 10 sites. Quarterly audit goal: 95%+ inventory accuracy. Current state: 78% accuracy (22% of devices have wrong location, missing serial, or not tracked). Improvement plan: 1) Enable SNMP polling for auto-discovery — discovers 90% of devices automatically (name, model, serial, software version), 2) Manual audit for physical location (walk each site, verify rack position against NetBox), 3) Cable management: document every patch panel-to-switch connection (critical for troubleshooting and maintenance planning), 4) EOL tracking: NetBox reports show 15% of devices past EOL — creates a refresh project. Results after 3 months: inventory accuracy reaches 96%. When a core switch fails: NOC checks NetBox, finds there are 3 hot spares (same model) in the DC spares cabinet, serial numbers match, and the switch is under warranty (support contract via CDW-G, expires 2026). New switch configured and installed in 45 minutes. Without inventory: would need to find a spare manually (unknown if available), check warranty (unknown), and locate the correct replacement (unknown) — adding 2+ hours to repair time.
theory.summary: Network inventory management is the foundation for effective NOC operations, procurement, and lifecycle management. Use NetBox or DCIM platforms to track devices, locations, serials, software versions, and warranty status. Combine auto-discovery (SNMP scanning) with periodic physical audits for 95%+ accuracy. Good inventory is essential for fast incident response, accurate capacity planning, and compliant asset management.

theory.what: Log analysis extracts actionable insights from the massive volume of logs generated by network devices (syslog), firewalls, servers, and applications. Techniques include: pattern matching with regex (find specific events like 'BGP-5-ADJCHANGE'), aggregation and counting (how many failed logins per hour?), timeline analysis (what happened before the incident — 5 minutes before, 1 minute before, during), correlation (cross-referencing syslog with monitoring data), and statistical anomaly detection (baseline normal behavior, flag deviations).
theory.why: A single network device generates 1000s of log messages per day. Across 500 devices: 5M+ log lines/day. Finding the 10 lines relevant to an incident is finding a needle in a haystack without proper techniques. Log analysis is essential for: root cause analysis (what happened and when), security forensics (who accessed what and when), troubleshooting (correlating symptoms with log events), and compliance (retaining logs with searchable format).
theory.how: Centralized logging with a SIEM (Security Information and Event Management) system: rsyslog receivers collect syslog from devices, forward to Splunk/ELK/Graylog for indexing and search. Effective queries use: time-bounded search (narrow timeframe around incident), keyword filtering (interface name, IP, error code), exclusion rules (remove known noise), and pattern-based grouping (group similar events). Example: Splunk search 'index=network sourcetype=syslog BGP *down* earliest=-30m' finds all BGP down events in the last 30 minutes.
theory.when: Log analysis is essential during: incident response (find root cause in logs), security investigations (did the attacker access this device?), compliance audits (produce logs for the audit period), capacity planning (log growth rate, disk space planning for log storage), and troubleshooting intermittent issues (logs that correlate with symptom occurrences).
key_concepts: Centralized syslog (all devices send to one server)
SIEM platforms: Splunk, ELK (Elasticsearch, Logstash, Kibana), Graylog
Regex pattern matching for complex log filtering
Time-bounded search (narrow incident time range)
Threshold-based alerting (X failed logins in N minutes → alert)
Log rotation and retention (90-365 days based on compliance)
Anomaly detection using baselines (hourly/daily/weekly patterns)
theory.configuration:
# rsyslog configuration
$template network_logs,"/var/log/network/%HOSTNAME%/%$year%-%$month%-%$day%.log"
:fromhost-ip, !isequal, "127.0.0.1" ?network_logs
# Device sends to syslog-ng:
logging host 10.0.0.100 transport udp port 514

logging facility local7
troubleshooting: Too many logs: set appropriate logging levels (informational on critical devices, errors only on access switches), use log rate-limiting
Cannot find relevant logs: broaden time window, search for related keywords (interface name, neighbor IP, error message), correlate across devices
Log retention filling disk: implement rotation (logrotate), tiered storage (hot 30 days → warm 90 days → cold 1 year), compression
Time synchronization issues: verify NTP on all devices — mismatched timestamps make correlation impossible
SIEM search too slow: optimize search queries (time-bounded, narrow index scope), use summary indexing for common searches
theory.worked_examples: Scenario: Users report intermittent connectivity issues between 10 AM and 11 AM. No current outage. Log analysis: 1) Search syslog for 'interface' and 'down' between 9:30 AM and 11:30 AM — 3 results found: interface Gig0/1 on Access-SW-05 flapped up/down 3 times between 10:15-10:45. 2) Search Access-SW-05 logs for 'errdisable' — found 'psecure-violation' on Gig0/1 at 10:15, 10:25, 10:35 (port security violation mode shutdown). 3) The port automatically recovers (errdisable recovery interval 300 seconds), causing the intermittent connectivity symptom. 4) Search for the connected device MAC (from port security logs) — it's a new printer that was moved from another port without the MAC being added to the allowed list. 5) Add MAC to allowed list, problem solved. Without centralized syslog search: engineers would need to SSH to each switch and check individual log buffers (only 4K entries, earlier events already rolled over). The 15-minute resolution becomes 2+ hours. Key: the timeline visualization in Kibana showed the interface flapping pattern was exactly 10 minutes apart (coinciding with the errdisable recovery interval), which immediately suggested port security violation as the root cause.
theory.summary: Log analysis is critical for root cause investigation and security forensics. Implement centralized syslog collection from all network devices to a SIEM platform (Splunk, ELK, Graylog). Master time-bounded search, keyword filtering, and pattern grouping. Set appropriate logging levels to balance detail with volume. Ensure all devices have synchronized time via NTP for accurate cross-device correlation.
